title: Chapter 3.  History — Tribal Uprisings Against British Rule

blocks.content: This is Jharkhand's single most exam-critical history chapter. The region was the site of some of colonial India's earliest, most sustained, and most significant tribal uprisings against British rule and exploitative land-revenue/moneylending systems - predating, and in several respects foreshadowing, the better-known 1857 Revolt. Expect detailed questions on each named uprising and its leader.

The common underlying cause across nearly all of Jharkhand's tribal uprisings was land alienation and economic exploitation: British colonial revenue policies, combined with the arrival of non-tribal moneylenders, traders and zamindars (collectively referred to in tribal terminology as 'Dikus', or outsiders), progressively dispossessed tribal cultivators of their traditional communal land rights, replacing customary tribal land-tenure systems with individual, revenue-extractive landholding patterns that heavily favoured outside landlords and moneylenders.

This pattern of land alienation, indebtedness, and the erosion of traditional tribal self-governance (through village heads/'Manki-Munda' systems, see Chapter 6) forms the direct thread connecting each of the successive uprisings detailed below, even though they occurred at different times, in different specific locations, and were led by different communities.

★ EXAM POINT: 'Dikus' - the tribal term for non-tribal outsiders (moneylenders, traders, zamindars) - is a key vocabulary term appearing across virtually every Jharkhand tribal-uprising question; understanding this term is essential to understanding the shared root cause of all the uprisings below.

cells: Chuar community (Jungle Mahals area, straddling present Jharkhand-West Bengal border)
One of the earliest tribal uprisings against East India Company revenue policy
Kol tribal community, led by figures including Buddhu Bhagat
Major uprising against land alienation to outside landlords/moneylenders in the Chota Nagpur region
Bhumij tribal community, led by Ganga Narayan Singh
Closely followed and linked in spirit to the Kol Rebellion, in the Manbhum/Singhbhum area
Santhal community, led by the brothers Sidho and Kanhu Murmu (with Chand and Bhairav)
One of the most significant tribal uprisings in Indian colonial history; led to the creation of the separate Santhal Pargana administrative area to address land-alienation grievances

A prolonged, more constitutional/agitational (less overtly armed) phase of resistance seeking restoration of tribal land rights through petitions and limited resistance, preceding the more famous Birsa Munda uprising
The most famous of all Jharkhand's tribal uprisings; combined armed resistance with religious/social reform; led directly to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 (Chapter 6)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Sequence to remember: Chuar Rebellion (1760s-1800s) -> Kol Rebellion (1831-32) -> Bhumij Revolt (1832-33) -> Santhal Hul (1855-56) -> Sardari Larai (1858-1890s) -> Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (1899-1900). This chronological sequence, spanning nearly a century and a half, is one of the highest-yield timeline questions in Jharkhand history.

Birsa Munda (1875-1900) is Jharkhand's single most important historical figure and a nationally recognised icon of tribal resistance - born in Ulihatu village (present-day Khunti district), he emerged as a religious reformer preaching a monotheistic faith ('Birsait' faith, blending elements of tribal religion with reformist critique of both Hindu and Christian missionary influence) before transforming into the leader of an armed uprising ('Ulgulan', meaning 'The Great Tumult' or 'The Great Revolt') against British rule and landlord exploitation in 1899-1900.

The Ulgulan sought to establish 'Munda Raj' (self-rule for the Munda people) and directly targeted symbols of British administrative and missionary presence, alongside oppressive landlords; British forces suppressed the uprising with considerable force, and Birsa Munda was captured in February 1900 and died in Ranchi jail on 9 June 1900 (officially of cholera, though the circumstances remain a subject of historical scrutiny and popular suspicion of foul play).

Despite its military suppression, the Ulgulan had a lasting, directly traceable legislative legacy: it was a major catalyst for the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, which formally recognised and protected tribal land rights against alienation to non-tribals - making Birsa Munda's movement one of the very few colonial-era tribal uprisings to produce a direct, lasting protective legal reform (Chapter 6).

Birsa Munda is commemorated today as 'Bhagwan' (God) Birsa Munda in popular tribal memory, with his birth anniversary (15 November) declared a national holiday - 'Janjatiya Gaurav Divas' (Tribal Pride Day) - since 2021, and his portrait hangs in the Indian Parliament's Central Hall, a rare honour reflecting his singular national stature among tribal leaders.

cells: Chotanagpur Tenancy Act enacted (direct legislative legacy of the Ulgulan)
Janjatiya Gaurav Divas declared (Birsa Munda's birth anniversary, 15 November)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Jharkhand's formation date itself (15 November 2000, Chapter 4) was deliberately chosen to coincide with Birsa Munda's birth anniversary - connecting this chapter directly to the state's very creation, and now also to the national 'Janjatiya Gaurav Divas' observance since 2021. This triple coincidence of dates (birth anniversary = state formation day = national Tribal Pride Day) is an extremely high-yield exam fact.

items: 'Dikus' = tribal term for non-tribal outsiders (moneylenders, traders, zamindars) - root cause of land alienation across all uprisings.

Key uprisings in order: Chuar Rebellion, Kol Rebellion (1831-32), Bhumij Revolt (1832-33, Ganga Narayan), Santhal Hul (1855-56, Sidho-Kanhu), Sardari Larai (1858-1890s), Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (1899-1900).
Santhal Hul (1855-56) led to the creation of the separate Santhal Pargana area.
Birsa Munda (1875-1900): led the Ulgulan; died in Ranchi jail, 9 June 1900; his movement directly led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908.
15 November = Birsa Munda's birth anniversary = Jharkhand's Formation Day (2000) = national Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (since 2021) - a triple-coincidence date.
